handback.t:
Full write-up with citations: C:\Users\mariu\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-mariu\8f3352b3-40ab-4151-abc9-d1de1978973c\scratchpad\agents-alt-paradigms.md (research date 2026-10-05; read-only work, no installs or code changes).

**Bottom line:** There is no fundamentally different paradigm a small team can own. Most of the interesting science needs frontier-lab compute, data and weight control. What a startup can own is the product layer: making an agent dependable at one narrow job, with proof.

**Paradigm by paradigm**
- **Neurosymbolic / formal verification:**
  - Real wins are in math and code, where a Lean checker gives an exact reward. AlphaProof reached IMO 2024 silver. Harmonic's Aristotle and ByteDance's Seed-Prover reached gold-equivalent on IMO 2025 with Lean-verified proofs.
  - Enterprise "neuro-symbolic agents" are mostly 2026 architecture or position papers (arxiv 2604.00555, 2606.13405). I found no production-scale wins outside verifiable domains.
  - Realistic use: deterministic guards and policy checks around the LLM, in domains with a checkable spec.
- **World models:**
  - AMI Labs (LeCun) raised a $1.03B seed in March 2026 for JEPA-style models (HPCwire).
  - The work targets physical and video domains. The LLM-agent versions are academic and I did not verify their gains.
  - Buildable version: sandboxes and simulators for software agents. A learned general world model is not.
- **Continual learning:**
  - Still unsolved at LLM scale. Continual RL shows severe catastrophic forgetting (arxiv 2607.04364). A 2026 paper reports self-evolving agents lose earlier capability as they adapt (arxiv 2605.09315, read via an LLM-summarized fetch, so the details are medium confidence).
  - Test-time training is reported to undermine safety guardrails (ICLR 2026 workshop, from a search snippet).
  - My inference on why it stays unsolved: weight interference, per-customer serving cost, regressions that are hard to detect, and no weight access to frontier models.
  - Google's Nested Learning / HOPE (NeurIPS 2025) is a proof of concept with no official implementation, so treat it as a watch item.
  - The buildable alternative is training-free learning from stored experience, for example JitRL (ICLR 2026).
- **Memory:**
  - Mem0, Zep and Letta are productized, and the labs are shipping memory as a platform feature.
  - Vendor LoCoMo and LongMemEval scores (90%+) are self-reported and not comparable. An independent audit reportedly found the lenient LLM judge accepts up to 63% of wrong answers.
  - Generic memory is commoditizing. Domain memory with provenance and correction is more defensible.
- **Small models and routing:**
  - NVIDIA's position paper (arxiv 2506.02153) argues most agent subtasks are narrow, so small distilled models plus a router with a large-model fallback is the right design. Its ~10-30x cost claim is the authors' own.
  - Buildable, using your own production traces. It is an optimization, not a moat, because the frontier moves fast.
- **Agent-as-compiler / program synthesis:**
  - AlphaEvolve and the Darwin Gödel Machine need a cheap, trustworthy automatic evaluator, and their gains are benchmark-bound.
  - The practical pattern is to have the LLM write a verified deterministic workflow once, then run that instead of re-planning. It gives cheaper, auditable runs and fewer compounding errors, but it is a thin moat alone.
- **What actually limits agents today:** reliability.
  - 95% per-step accuracy gives about 36% over 20 steps.
  - Tau-bench reported GPT-4o at 61% pass@1 but 25% pass^8.
  - METR time horizons double every 3-7 months, so the labs are improving the base model quickly. METR figures here are secondhand.

**Feasibility verdict, ranked by defensibility for a small team**
1. A vertical workflow-owning agent with proprietary data: integrations, exception handling, audit trail, domain evals, customer trust, and responsibility for a completed outcome. This is where the sources agree the moat is, though they are blogs and opinion.
2. A reliability and control layer: evals, traces, regression gates, guardrails, human approvals. Observability firms and model vendors are moving into it, so it needs domain depth.
3. Compile-to-workflow execution.
4. Domain memory plus trace-based learning without weight updates.
5. Distilled small models for your own high-volume subtasks.
6. Formal verification, only where a checkable spec exists. It is a feature of a vertical product, not a horizontal one.

**Not realistic to out-build:**
- A better foundation model or architecture.
- Real continual learning of model weights.
- A general world model.
- General long-horizon autonomy through new training.
- Generic memory, tool use or connectors.
- "Self-evolving agent swarm" claims without a strong external evaluator.

**On the user's goal:** "Creating intelligent AI agents" splits in two.
- **Buildable:** a frontier model wrapped with tools, verification, memory, evals and routing so it succeeds reliably at a narrow job, with a measured pass^k on real customer tasks.
- **Not buildable:** "new intelligence", meaning better underlying reasoning, learning or world understanding. Any startup claim of that kind built on a frontier API is really a prompt, scaffold or retrieval improvement and should be measured as one.
- **Suggested path:** pick one vertical and one outcome, build the eval set from real tasks first, then add compile-to-workflow, routing and trace-based memory only where the evals show they pay off. Track nested learning, world models and test-time training as things to swap in when the labs ship them.

**Caveats:**
- Several 2026 arXiv papers were seen only as search snippets, so I did not read their experiments.
- The market-structure sources are blogs, and the "80-95% of wrappers fail" statistic is unsourced.
- The METR figure is secondhand.
